knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,

```{r library}
library(diplomacyR)
```

This vignette is for people who want to extend the package, read its source,
or understand why it is put together the way it is. Nothing here is needed to
play a game.

## Six classes

Everything in the package is one of six S3 classes. They are all plain lists
or tibbles underneath, deliberately: a user who wants to reach in and take
something out should be able to, without learning an accessor API.

| Class | What it is | Built by |
|---|---|---|
| `dp_map` | the board: provinces, both adjacency graphs, supply and home centres, the opening position | `dp_map()` |
| `dp_game` | one position at one moment: units, ownership, season, year, phase, anything awaiting retreat | `dp_new_game()`, `dp_game_from_units()` |
| `dp_orders` | a set of orders, one per row | `dp_order()`, `dp_parse_orders()`, `dp_legal_orders()` |
| `dp_result` | what a phase did: per-order success, new positions, dislodgements, standoffs | `dp_adjudicate()`, `dp_retreat()`, `dp_build()` |
| `dp_history` | a whole game, turn by turn | `dp_history()`, `dp_play()` |
| `dp_sim` | a batch of games and their outcomes | `dp_simulate()` |

The pipeline is a loop over three of them. A `dp_game` plus a `dp_orders`
goes into an adjudicator, which returns a `dp_result`; `dp_advance()` turns
the game and the result into the next `dp_game`. `dp_step()` is that loop
body, `dp_play()` is the loop, `dp_history` is its log and `dp_sim` is a pile
of logs reduced to numbers.

```{r structure}
names(dp_new_game())
```

```{r structure-result}
result <- dp_adjudicate(dp_new_game(), dp_example_orders())
names(result)
```

`dp_orders` is the one class that is also a tibble, because orders are
genuinely tabular and people want to filter and join them.

```{r orders-class}
class(dp_example_orders())
```

## Constructor, validator, helper

Each class follows the same three-function pattern.

* `new_dp_*()` is the **constructor**: it takes trusted, already-correct
  components and attaches the class. It is internal, cheap, and does no
  checking, so the hot paths in the engine can build objects freely.
* `validate_dp_*()` is the **validator**: it takes a candidate object and
  checks the invariants that the rest of the package is entitled to assume.
  For a `dp_game` those are that no province holds two units, that every unit
  stands somewhere legal for its type, that supply-centre ownership refers to
  real centres and real powers, and that the season and phase are ones the
  phase machine knows.
* `dp_*()` is the **helper**: the exported, user-facing function that takes
  convenient arguments, coerces them, and returns a validated object.

So `dp_game_from_units()` will refuse to build a nonsense position, while the
adjudicator's internals build unvalidated intermediates thousands of times a
second without paying for the checks.

```{r validate, error = TRUE}
dp_game_from_units(data.frame(
  power = c("France", "Germany"),
  type = c("army", "army"),
  loc = c("par", "par")
))
```

Errors are raised with **cli** and carry the calling function's environment,
so the message points at the function the user called rather than at whatever
internal helper noticed the problem. Every user-facing function takes a
`call` argument for that purpose.

Each class also has an `is_dp_*()` predicate, and the printing methods you
would expect.

```{r methods}
methods(class = "dp_game")
```

`format()` gives a one-line summary suitable for embedding, `print()` a
readable block, and `summary()` a tibble rather than a printed object — so
`summary()` on a result is the per-order outcome table, and `summary()` on a
simulation is `dp_stats()`.

Analysis output is tibbles and plot output is **ggplot2** objects, without
exception. Neither ever prints as a side effect, so both compose.

## Why the adjudicator guesses

Diplomacy is adjudicated simultaneously, and the rules are genuinely
circular. Whether a support holds depends on whether the attack on the
supporting unit succeeds; whether that attack succeeds depends on what
supports it; and those supports may in turn be cut by the first unit. There
is no evaluation order that resolves every position, because for some
positions no order exists.

The engine therefore uses the standard guess-and-check resolver described by
Lucas B. Kruijswijk. To resolve an order it:

1. marks the order as *being guessed*, provisionally `FALSE`, and adjudicates
   it;
2. records every order that was consulted while still in the guessing
   state — the dependency stack;
3. if nothing provisional was consulted, the answer is final;
4. otherwise re-adjudicates the same order under the opposite guess, `TRUE`;
5. if both guesses agree, the answer is final regardless of the cycle;
6. if they disagree, the orders form a genuine cycle, and a backup rule
   breaks it.

Steps 1 to 5 settle the overwhelming majority of positions, including all the
merely awkward ones. The backup rule handles the two cases the rulebook
itself does not fully determine:

* **Circular movement.** If every order in the cycle is a move — a ring of
  units each stepping into the province the next one is vacating — they all
  succeed.
* **A convoy paradox.** If any order in the cycle is a convoy, the convoys in
  the cycle are disrupted. This is the Szykman rule, and it is the resolution
  the Diplomacy Adjudicator Test Cases mark as preferred. `vignette("adjudication")` works through the classic example.

The dependency stack is what makes this tractable. Without it the resolver
would have to guess about every order in the position; with it, it only ever
guesses about the handful of orders that actually depend on each other, and
it unwinds the stack as soon as a sub-problem is settled.

Convoy paths are resolved lazily for the same reason. A convoyed move needs
an unbroken chain of fleets, each ordered to convoy that exact move and none
of them dislodged; the search walks the chain depth-first and resolves a
convoy order only at the moment the path actually needs it, so a fleet on an
irrelevant branch never enters the dependency stack at all.

Order strength is expressed as the four quantities the rules imply — hold,
attack, defend and prevent strength — and a move succeeds only when its
attack strength *strictly* exceeds the relevant opposition. Every tie
bounces. That single asymmetry is what produces standoffs, beleaguered
garrisons and the two prohibitions on acting against one's own units, without
any of them needing a special case.

## How coasts are modelled

Coasts are where most Diplomacy engines get untidy, so they are worth a
section.

The board carries **two adjacency graphs**, not one. Armies move on a graph
of provinces; fleets move on a graph of *locations*, where a location is
either a province or a named coast of a province. The two are queried
separately.

```{r graphs}
dp_adjacent(dp_map(), "spa", "army")
dp_adjacent(dp_map(), "spa/nc", "fleet")
dp_adjacent(dp_map(), "spa/sc", "fleet")
```

Spain's two coasts have different neighbours and a fleet cannot sail between
them, which is exactly what the split-location representation encodes. Only
three provinces on the standard board need it: Spain, Bulgaria and St
Petersburg.

A location is written `province/coast`, and two internal helpers do all the
work: one strips a location down to its province, the other extracts the
coast. Almost everything in the engine — occupancy, support, standoffs,
dislodgement — is decided at province level, because the rules are about
provinces. Only fleet movement, and the choice of destination coast, look at
the coast.

That is why support works the way it does. A support directed into Spain
backs a fleet moving to either Spanish coast, since the support is about the
province; but a support that *names* a coast has to name the right one.

A fleet's location must be unambiguous when it is created:

```{r coast-error, error = TRUE}
dp_unit("Russia", "fleet", "spa")
```

but a coast that is forced is filled in silently, both when a unit is
constructed and when a move is adjudicated. A fleet ordered from Gascony to
Spain can only be arriving on the north coast, so that is where it goes:

```{r coast-fill}
gascony <- dp_game_from_units(
  data.frame(power = "France", type = "fleet", loc = "gas")
)
dp_adjudicate(gascony, "France: F Gas - Spa")$orders
```

A fleet in the Mid-Atlantic Ocean touches both coasts, so the same order
there is ambiguous, and an ambiguous order is void:

```{r coast-ambiguous}
atlantic <- dp_game_from_units(
  data.frame(power = "France", type = "fleet", loc = "mao")
)
res <- dp_adjudicate(atlantic, "France: F Mao - Spa")
summary(res)[, c("loc", "type", "target", "note")]
```

Coordinates for the plot are stored per coast as well, so a fleet on the
south coast of Spain is drawn in the right place rather than in the middle of
the country.

## Performance notes

The engine is written to be run hundreds of thousands of times, which shapes
a few decisions that would otherwise look odd.

* The standard board is parsed from JSON once and cached for the session, and
  the sea and coastal neighbourhoods the convoy code walks constantly are
  precomputed at load rather than derived on demand.
* `dp_legal_orders()` accumulates chunks of columns and binds them once
  instead of building a tibble per candidate order. Enumerating legal orders
  is on the hot path for every bot and every turn of every simulated game,
  and the row-wise version is orders of magnitude slower.
* The resolver keeps its state in an environment rather than a list, so that
  the recursive functions can update the guess state in place without copying
  the position at every step.

Everything above is internal. The public surface is the six classes, the
adjudicators, the phase machine and the analysis functions; the rest can be
rewritten without notice.
